The river doesn’t stop

Information overload is almost five hundred years old. The best answer to it is more than two thousand.

DJ, founderOctober 29, 20265 min read

Most mornings on the L train I do the same small, silly thing. I open my phone, see a number in a red circle, and feel my chest tighten before I’ve read a word. The number is never the problem. It’s the feeling that the water is rising and I’m supposed to be bailing.

I used to think that was a modern problem. It turns out to be one of the oldest problems people who think for a living have, and the best answer to it is more than two thousand years old.

1545

In 1545 a Swiss scholar named Conrad Gessner published the Bibliotheca universalis, an attempt to list every book in Latin, Greek and Hebrew. He got to roughly ten thousand titles. Along the way he complained about what he called “that confusing and harmful abundance of books,” a line the historian Ann Blair, in Too Much to Know, uses to show how early the feeling of overload set in.

That was about ninety years after Gutenberg. The flood had barely started.

Every generation since has had its own version: too many books, then too many newspapers, then too many channels, now too many tabs. The volume changes. The feeling doesn’t. Which suggests the answer was never going to be less information. The river doesn’t stop.

Two ways to stop a flood

There’s an old Chinese story about this. It’s about a father and a son.

Long ago, the legend goes, great floods covered the land. The first man given the job of ending them was Gun. He built dikes and dams, walls to hold the water back. For nine years he built them higher, and for nine years the water went over them or around them. He failed.

His son Yu took over, and Yu didn’t build walls. He dug channels. He studied where the water wanted to go and gave it somewhere to go, dredging riverbeds and cutting paths to the sea. It took thirteen years. The story says he walked past his own front door three times without going in. The floods ended, and he’s remembered as Yu the Great.

Chinese has a word for each method. 堵 is to block. 疏 is to clear a path. Nearly every productivity system I’ve tried was Gun’s. Inbox zero, notification bans, the weekend digital detox: walls, all of them. They hold for a few days, and then the water goes over.

The weir at Dujiangyan

If Yu is legend, Li Bing is history.

Around 256 BC, Li Bing governed Shu, in what’s now Sichuan, for the state of Qin. Every spring the Min River came down out of the mountains swollen with snowmelt and flooded the Chengdu plain. In other seasons there wasn’t enough water. The obvious fix was a dam.

Li Bing didn’t build one. He built Dujiangyan, and more than twenty-two centuries later it’s still working.

None of its parts stops the river. A long island shaped like a fish’s mouth sits in the current and splits it in two: an outer river that carries floods on past, and an inner river that feeds the fields. The riverbed is shaped so that in the dry season most of the water turns inside, and in flood season most of it goes out. Downstream, a spillway lets extra water and silt spill back out of the inner channel before they reach the farms. And a narrow gap cut through a hill, called the Bottle-Neck, caps how much can ever pass into the plain.

The river keeps doing what rivers do, and the plain gets a steady, usable share of it. The Chengdu plain has been called 天府之国, the Land of Abundance, for most of the time since.

That’s the design I want for my own head.

Notebooks are weirs

Thinkers built their own small Dujiangyans long ago. They just called them notebooks.

Renaissance students kept commonplace books, copying passages under headings so they could find them again. An English translation of John Locke’s method for indexing one came out in 1706 and was copied and adapted for a century after. In the twentieth century the sociologist Niklas Luhmann kept a slip box of some ninety thousand index cards, numbered and linked, and described it as a partner he could talk to.

None of these held back the reading. They split it. Most of what Luhmann read went on by. A small, steady part went into the box, where it waited, sorted, until he needed it.

The unfinished thing that won’t leave

There’s a reason this matters beyond tidiness.

The story goes that in the 1920s the psychologist Kurt Lewin noticed a waiter who remembered every unpaid order in detail and forgot each one the moment the bill was settled. His student Bluma Zeigarnik tested it in the lab and found that people remember interrupted tasks better than finished ones. Unfinished things stay switched on.

That’s the red circle on the L train: all the open loops it stands for, humming at once.

In 2011 E. J. Masicampo and Roy Baumeister ran a series of studies on those loops. People with an unfinished goal on their mind did worse on unrelated tasks, because the goal kept intruding. But people who got to write down a specific plan for it stopped being distracted, even though they hadn’t finished anything. Putting it somewhere, with a next step attached, was enough to let the mind set it down.

David Allen, who built a whole method on this, says it more simply: your mind is for having ideas, not holding them.

A fish mouth, not a dam

So here’s what I think a board like Nook is for, when it works.

It isn’t a dam. It won’t stop anything coming at you, and it shouldn’t try. It’s the fish’s mouth. The small part of the river that belongs to something you’re actually doing gets split off into a place where it can sit still, arranged well enough that your head can let go of it. The rest goes by, and that’s fine. It was always going to.

The farmers on the Chengdu plain never needed less river. They needed the right amount of it, moving at the right speed.

Most of us need about the same: a few quiet channels, each one running to a field we’re actually tending.
